Neonatal American badgers emerge from the womb after a gestation period of 41 days [tg = 41 days] when maternal body temperature is maintained at approximately 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a relatively brief intrauterine development for a mustelid of this size. Newborn pups weigh a mere 93.5 grams [Wwb = 93.5 grams] at birth, reflecting the altricial state of the neonatal mammal. This low birth mass places the species well below the expected neonatal mass for carnivores of comparable adult size, a pattern that likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the female's solitary, fossorial lifestyle. The suckling juvenile remains entirely dependent on maternal milk for the first several weeks of life, during which a period of accelerated mass gain compensates for the modest starting point. Field observations indicate that the time since birth at weaning, when the pup transitions to solid food, occurs at approximately 56 days since birth [tx = approximately 56 days since birth] under typical thermal conditions of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], marking the onset of nutritional independence and the beginning of the juvenile stage.

Female badgers ultimately attain a maximum adult body mass of approximately 7,200 grams [Wwi = approximately 7,200 grams], whereas males are considerably larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of about 8,600 grams [Wwi = about 8,600 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is characteristic of the species and is thought to be linked to male-male competition for breeding territories during the mating season. Northern subspecies, however, can exceed these values considerably, with some individuals approaching 9.5 kilograms for females and 11.5 to 15 kilograms for males, underscoring the influence of geographic variation and prey abundance on asymptotic body size. At the other end of the developmental spectrum, the wet weight at weaning for a successfully weaned juvenile is approximately 3,000 grams [Wwx = approximately 3,000 grams], representing a striking increase from the 93.5 grams at birth. This roughly 32-fold increase in body mass over the course of about 8 weeks underscores the intensity of maternal investment in the single annual litter.

Reproductive output in the American badger is relatively modest for a carnivore of its body mass and reflects a slow life-history pace. Females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with a mean litter size of three pups per litter [N_R_i = three pups per litter], yielding an annual reproductive output of three pups per year. This low fecundity is counterbalanced by a high degree of maternal care and the altricial nature of the offspring. The timing of first reproduction is closely tied to the attainment of sexual maturity, which differs markedly between the sexes. For females, the time since birth at puberty is 183 days [tp = 183 days], meaning that a female born in early spring could theoretically reach reproductive maturity by early autumn of her first year at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. However, first successful breeding is often deferred until the following spring due to the seasonal nature of mating opportunities in temperate regions.

Males, in contrast, experience a considerably prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching reproductive maturity. The time since birth at puberty for males extends to 441 days [tp = 441 days], meaning that a male born in one spring will not become reproductively active until the summer of his second year at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This delayed maturation is consistent with the extended period required to attain the substantially larger body size characteristic of adult males, which is prerequisite for successful competition for access to females. The prolonged juvenile phase in males allows for the accumulation of both skeletal mass and fat reserves necessary to survive the winter denning period and emerge in condition to challenge resident territorial males. This two-year delay in male reproductive maturity results in a relatively low maximum reproductive rate for the species.

Under ideal thermal conditions, with a maternal body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] and abundant food resources, the maximum reproductive rate is realized through a combination of three pups per litter [N_R_i = three pups per litter] and approximately 0.7 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.7 litters per year]. Longevity records for the American badger indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] under favorable conditions when body temperature is maintained at 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This substantial lifespan, coupled with delayed male maturity and low annual fecundity, positions the badger firmly within the slow end of the mustelid life-history continuum. The extended reproductive window afforded by a long life allows females to compensate for low per-event output over many breeding seasons, while the relatively late age at first reproduction for males ensures that only the largest, most competitive individuals contribute genetically to the next generation.
